content: The Lourdes Medical Bureau is a medical organization located in Lourdes, France. It operates as an official entity within the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes but is exclusively managed and staffed by physicians. Its primary and most renowned role is the rigorous medical evaluation of reported cures associated with the Lourdes shrine. The term Medical Bureau also refers to a specific assembly of doctors convened to investigate claims of unexplained healings. Historical Background The apparitions at Lourdes occurred between February 11 and July 16, 1858. Following these events, reports of seemingly miraculous cures began to emerge. In 1859, Professor Henri Vergez, from the Faculty of Medicine at Montpellier, was appointed as the medical consultant to the Episcopal Commission of Inquiry to assess these claims. Vergez concluded that seven cases were genuinely inexplicable, leading to calls for the Roman Catholic Church to recognize these events as miracles. In 1883, a group of doctors affiliated with the sanctuary established the Bureau des Constatations Médicales, which served as the precursor to the current Medical Bureau. Its first leader was Baron Dunot de Saint-Maclou. In 1905, Pope Pius X mandated that claims of miraculous cures at Lourdes undergo a formal and rigorous investigative process. This directive led to the establishment of the Lourdes Medical Bureau. Current Administration The Lourdes Medical Bureau is headed by a single physician. The current director is Dr. Patrick Theillier. The bureau operates from a modest office located on the second floor of the Accueil Jean Paul II building within the Domain, the consecrated area surrounding the shrine. Physicians practicing in or visiting Lourdes can apply for membership in the bureau. Additionally, healthcare professionals such as nurses, physiotherapists, and pharmacists are also eligible to join. Members are provided with a distinctive badge featuring a red cross on a white background with the word Credo (I believe) inscribed above it. Membership is open to individuals of any religious belief or none. Members are encouraged to inform the bureau of their visits to Lourdes. The bureau publishes a quarterly journal, Fons Vitae (Fountain of Life), which is distributed to its members. It also circulates case reports of interest for review. Investigation of Apparent Cures Each year, approximately 35 claims of healing are brought to the attention of the Lourdes Medical Bureau. Most of these are dismissed after initial review. However, three to five cases annually undergo more detailed investigation. When a claim warrants further scrutiny, a Medical Bureau is convened, comprising doctors present in Lourdes at the time of the reported cure. This underscores the importance of members notifying the bureau of their visits. The investigation involves a thorough review of the patient’s medical history, including case notes and diagnostic test results such as biopsies, imaging studies (e.g., X-rays, CT scans), and laboratory findings. If the Medical Bureau determines that further investigation is justified, the case is referred to the International Lourdes Medical Committee (Comité Médical International de Lourdes, or CMIL). This committee consists of approximately 20 medical experts from various specialties and countries, representing diverse religious beliefs. The investigator may also consult with colleagues. The findings are presented at a CMIL meeting, which is attended by the head of the Lourdes Medical Bureau and the Bishop of Tarbes and Lourdes (currently Jacques Perrier). The individual who experienced the cure is typically not present. For a cure to be deemed medically inexplicable, the following criteria must be met: 1. The original diagnosis must be verified and confirmed beyond doubt. 2. The condition must be considered incurable with current medical knowledge and treatments (though ongoing treatments do not disqualify the case). 3. The cure must occur in association with a visit to Lourdes, typically while at or near the shrine (though drinking or bathing in the water is not a requirement). 4. The cure must be immediate, with rapid resolution of symptoms and signs of the illness. 5. The cure must be complete, leaving no residual impairment or deficit. 6. The cure must be permanent, with no recurrence of the condition. CMIL does not have the authority to declare a cure miraculous. It can only determine whether a cure is medically inexplicable. The final decision regarding the miraculous nature of a cure rests with the Church. Cases deemed medically inexplicable are referred to the bishop of the diocese where the individual resides. The bishop, in consultation with experts and the Vatican, decides whether to recognize the cure as a miracle. The bishop may reject the claim for any reason. Bishop Jacques Perrier of Tarbes and Lourdes has expressed a desire for a new approach to the recognition of cures at Lourdes, emphasizing that a pilgrimage to Mary is not solely about seeking miracles but is also a journey of love, prayer, and solidarity with the suffering community. Notable Cases Some cases dismissed by the Medical Bureau have nonetheless gained public attention. One such example is Jack Traynor. Below are examples of notable cases officially recognized as cures: Jeanne Fretel: A 31-year-old student nurse from Rennes, France, suffering from tubercular peritonitis with severe complications for seven years. She was comatose when brought to Lourdes on May 10, 1948. After receiving a fragment of the Eucharist, she awoke and reported being instantly and permanently cured. Her cure was officially recognized on November 11, 1950. Brother Léo Schwager: A 28-year-old from Fribourg, Switzerland, with multiple sclerosis for five years. He visited Lourdes on April 30, 1952, and his cure was recognized on December 18, 1960. Alice Couteault (née Alice Gourdon): A 34-year-old from Bouillé-Loretz, France, with multiple sclerosis for three years. She visited Lourdes on May 15, 1952, and her cure was recognized on July 16, 1956. Marie Bigot: A 32-year-old from La Richardais, France, with arachnoiditis of the posterior fossa, causing blindness, deafness, and hemiplegia. She visited Lourdes on October 8, 1953, and October 10, 1954. Her cure was recognized on August 15, 1956. Ginette Nouvel (née Ginette Fabre): A 26-year-old from Carmaux, France, with Budd-Chiari syndrome (supra-hepatic venous thrombosis). She visited Lourdes on September 21, 1954, and her cure was recognized on May 31, 1963. Elisa Aloi (later Elisa Varcalli): A 27-year-old from Patti, Italy, with tuberculous osteoarthritis and multiple fistulae in her right leg. She visited Lourdes on June 5, 1958, and her cure was recognized on May 26, 1965. Juliette Tamburini: A 22-year-old from Marseilles, France, with femoral osteoperiostitis and fistulae for ten years. She visited Lourdes on July 17, 1959, and her cure was recognized on May 11, 1965. Vittorio Micheli: A 23-year-old from Scurelle, Italy, with a pelvic sarcoma so advanced that his left thigh was detached from the hip socket, leaving his leg paralyzed. After taking the waters at Lourdes on June 1, 1963, he experienced pain relief and regained mobility. By February 1964, the tumor had disappeared, and his hip joint had recalcified. His cure was recognized on May 26, 1976. Serge Perrin: A 41-year-old from Lion D'Angers, France, with recurrent right hemiplegia and ocular lesions due to bilateral carotid artery disorders. He visited Lourdes on May 1, 1970, and experienced a sudden recovery, regaining vision and mobility. His cure was recognized on June 17, 1978. Delizia Cirolli (later Delizia Costa): A 12-year-old from Paterno, Italy, with Ewing's sarcoma of the right knee. Her mother refused amputation and took her to Lourdes on December 24, 1976. The tumor regressed completely, though her tibia required surgical correction. Her cure was recognized on June 28, 1989. Jean-Pierre Bély: A 51-year-old Frenchman with multiple sclerosis. He visited Lourdes on October 9, 1987, and his cure was recognized on February 9, 1999. Dr. Patrick Theillier Dr. Patrick Theillier is the twelfth physician to lead the Lourdes Medical Bureau. He earned his medical degree from Lille in 1964. Medical Care for Visitors The Lourdes Medical Bureau does not provide direct medical care to pilgrims or visitors. Instead, general practitioners and the local hospital in Lourdes are responsible for medical care. Many pilgrim groups bring their own volunteer healthcare providers, including doctors and nurses, to care for their members. The Domain includes a treatment area called the Dispensary, located in the Accueil Jean Paul II building. The Dispensary is equipped to handle minor injuries and acute medical issues, with facilities for resuscitation, airway management, and defibrillation. It also has a small electric ambulance. The Dispensary operates during daylight hours and is staffed by nurses.
